expectations.text: Claude identifies that manager motivation was measured after the treatment and therefore may be a mediator on the training → motivation → performance causal path
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly states: 'Manager motivation level, measured 1 month after the training ended, is almost certainly a mediator — a variable that sits on the causal pathway between the treatment (training) and the outcome (performance). The causal chain likely looks something like this: Management Training → Manager Motivation ↑ → Team Performance ↑'. Post-treatment timing is further emphasized: 'Manager motivation measured 1 month after training fails both conditions.'

expectations.text: Claude warns that controlling for a post-treatment mediator blocks the causal mechanism you're trying to measure, biasing the estimated training effect toward zero
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'When you include a mediator as a control variable in a regression, you are blocking the very pathway through which your treatment works. This is called overcontrol bias... your estimate of the training effect will be attenuated — you'll systematically underestimate how much the training actually improved performance, potentially to the point of finding no effect at all when there truly is one.' A concrete example reinforces the direction: 'If you control for motivation, your model asks: Among managers with the same motivation level, did training affect performance? The answer will be approximately zero — not because training doesn't work, but because you've conditioned away the effect.'

expectations.text: Claude distinguishes the total effect of training (including the motivation pathway) from the direct effect (net of motivation) — AND specifies which estimand is policy-relevant for the question at hand: if the goal is evaluating whether to scale the training program, the total effect is what matters; the direct effect is only relevant if you're trying to isolate mechanisms beyond the motivation pathway
expectations.evidence: The response mentions decomposing 'the total effect into direct and indirect (motivation-mediated) components' only in the context of mediation analysis as a secondary goal. It does not name or frame 'total effect' vs. 'direct effect' as distinct estimands that the analyst must choose between, and it never connects estimand choice to the policy decision at hand. There is no statement that the total effect is what matters for a scaling decision, nor that the direct effect is only relevant for mechanism investigation. The policy-relevance framing — the core of this expectation — is absent.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT recommend including post-treatment motivation as a control without raising this structural concern
expectations.evidence: The entire response is structured around warning against including motivation as a control. The only mention of inclusion is as a labeled sensitivity analysis: 'If a reviewer or stakeholder insists, you can report a sensitivity analysis with motivation included, but clearly label it as a potentially biased estimate and explain the direction of expected bias (downward attenuation of the training effect).' This is explicitly flagged as biased, fully satisfying the requirement.

claims.claim: Including a mediator as a control blocks the causal pathway and causes overcontrol bias (attenuation toward zero)
claims.evidence: Well-established in causal inference literature (Rosenbaum 1984, Pearl 2009). The response correctly names the bias, its mechanism, and its direction.

claims.claim: Manager motivation measured 1 month after training is almost certainly a post-treatment variable affected by the training
claims.evidence: The post-treatment timing alone justifies this inference; the response correctly flags it.

claims.claim: Formal mediation analysis (Imai et al. 2010) can decompose the total effect into direct and indirect components
claims.evidence: Accurate reference: Imai et al. 2010 introduced the causal mediation framework allowing this decomposition under sequential ignorability.

claims.claim: A powerful mediator included as a control causes more severe attenuation than a weak mediator
claims.evidence: Directionally correct: a variable that explains more variance in the outcome absorbs more of the treatment effect when improperly controlled for.

claims.claim: The primary model should include only pre-treatment covariates and omit post-treatment variables
claims.evidence: Standard and correct recommendation from a causal inference standpoint.

suggestions.assertion: Claude distinguishes the total effect of training (including the motivation pathway) from the direct effect (net of motivation) — AND specifies which estimand is policy-relevant for the question at hand
suggestions.reason: This is the most discriminating assertion in the eval, and it correctly fails here — the response warns about bias but never helps the analyst identify which estimand to target for their actual decision. Consider keeping this assertion as-is; it is hard to satisfy without doing the work correctly. One option is to split it into two assertions: one for the conceptual distinction (total vs. direct effect) and one for the policy-relevance framing, since a response can partially satisfy the first without the second — as this response demonstrates.

No assertion checks whether Claude provides concrete actionable next steps (e.g., recommending mediation analysis, restricting controls to pre-treatment variables). The response does this well, but it goes unverified. Adding an assertion on actionability — for example, 'Claude recommends mediation analysis as the appropriate framework rather than including motivation as a covariate' — would improve coverage.

No assertion checks whether Claude correctly characterizes the direction of bias (attenuation/downward bias toward zero). The response gets this right and it is a meaningful quality marker distinguishing a precise causal inference answer from a vague one.

eval_feedback.overall: The eval is well-targeted at the core structural error. Expectation 3 is the most discriminating and correctly identifies a real gap in this response. Splitting it into a conceptual-distinction assertion and a policy-relevance assertion would improve precision. Adding assertions on actionability and directional bias characterization would round out coverage.
